paragraphs.text: Delivered at the beginning of Lent, on "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth"; on fasting and almsgiving. On fasting and almsgiving. 1. Spring is pleasant to sailors, and pleasant to farmers too. But spring is not as pleasant to sailors or to farmers as the season of fasting is to those who wish to live the life of wisdom. The fast is the spiritual spring of souls, the true calm of our thoughts. Spring is pleasant to farmers because they then see the earth crowned with flowers, and the growth of the plants spread over it on every side like an embroidered garment. Spring is pleasant to sailors because they can sail the sea's broad back in safety, with the waves smoothed down, dolphins playing in the deep calm and often tumbling right alongside the ship. But the spring of fasting is pleasant to us because it stills waves for us, waves not of water but of irrational desires, and it sets on our heads a crown not of flowers but of spiritual graces. For it says, "You shall receive a crown of graces upon your head." The appearing of a swallow does not drive away winter the way the appearing of fasting drives the winter of the passions out of our minds. The soul no longer battles against the flesh, and the maidservant no longer rises up against her mistress; this whole war of the body has been brought to an end. Since there is great peace among us, then, and great calm, come, let us too launch the vessel of teaching, and carry your gentle ears from harbor to harbor. Come, let us venture on subtler thoughts and reflect on heaven and earth and sea and the rest of the body of creation, for these are what were read to us today. "And what does the account of creation have to do with us?" someone says. A great deal, beloved. For if the maker is perceived in proportion to the greatness and beauty of created things, then the longer we dwell on the greatness of their beauty, the further we are led by the hand toward their maker. It is a great good to know what a creature is and what the Creator is, what a work is and what its maker is. If the enemies of the truth had known how to distinguish these things precisely, they would not have thrown everything into confusion and turned it upside down. I do not mean that they brought the stars and the heaven down and raised the earth up. I mean that they brought the King of the heavens down from his royal throne and set him alongside creation, and honored creation with the seat of honor that belongs to the Godhead. If the Manichaeans had known how to reason rightly about creation, they would not have honored creation, which comes from nothing and is perishable, flowing and changeable, with the privileges of being unbegotten. If the Greeks had known how to reason rightly about creation, they would not have strayed from the truth, nor would they have worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator. The heaven is beautiful, but it was made so that you would worship the one who made it. The sun is bright, but it is there so that you would serve the one who fashioned it. If you are going to stop short at wonder over creation and be led astray [?] by the beauty of the works, then the light has become darkness for you, or rather by the light… [Notes: Reg. reads "calm, the anchor of the faithful, and toward God [?]", and that is how it should be read. Edd. read κυβιστ[?]. Reg. reads "first".]

…hear how the Prophet also speaks to them about those powers above. "Praise the Lord from the heavens," he says, "praise him in the heights; praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created." And what wonder is it that the Old Testament teaches this way, when in the New as well, at a time that called for loftier teachings, Paul took the same road in speaking to the Athenians that Moses took in instructing the Jews? For he did not speak to them about angels and archangels either, but about heaven and earth and sea. He addressed them like this: "God, who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands." But when he was speaking to the Philippians, he did not lead them along this road. He raised them to a loftier discourse, speaking like this: "For in him all things were created, those in the heavens and those on earth, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities; all things were created through him and for him." John did the same. Since his disciples were more mature, he spoke of the whole of creation at once. He did not say "heaven and earth and sea," but "All things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be that has come to be," whether visible, he means, or invisible. It is the same with teachers. The teacher who takes a child from its mother teaches it the first letters, while the teacher who takes over a pupil from another teacher leads him on to the loftier lessons. So it was with Moses, Paul and John. Moses took our nature when it knew nothing and had only just been weaned from milk, and he taught it the first letters of the knowledge of God. John and Paul received it as if from Moses its teacher, and they lead it up to loftier lessons, briefly reminding it of the earlier ones. Do you see the kinship of the two Testaments? Do you see how their teachings agree? You heard of the creation of sensible things in the Old Testament, and of the creation of intelligible things when David says, "For he spoke, and they came to be." In the same way, in the New, after speaking of the invisible powers, he spoke also of the sensible creation: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." This saying is short and plain, a single saying, yet it is able to overthrow all the towers of our opponents. Consider. A Manichaean comes and says, "Matter is unbegotten." Say to him, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," and you have overthrown all his conceit at once. "But he does not believe the word of Scripture," someone says. Then for that very reason repel him as a madman and turn away from him. For when someone does not believe God's own declaration, and condemns the truth as a lie, how is he not plainly displaying his unbelief as proof of madness? And how from nothing… [Notes: [?] gave themselves to piety. Hear — Reg. [?] of philosophical teachings — Reg.]

…those men have a [?] complexion, a lowered brow and gentle words. But flee the bait, and recognize the wolf hidden in the sheep's skin. Hate him most of all for this: toward you, his fellow servant, he seems mild and gentle, but toward the common Master of us all he is fiercer than rabid dogs. He brings an undeclared war and a truceless conflict against heaven, and sets up some power to oppose God. Flee the venom of wickedness, hate these deadly drugs. Hold fast, with great steadfastness, to the inheritance you received from the fathers: the faith and teaching that come from the divine Scriptures. "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." What is this? First the heaven, then the earth? First the roof, then the floor? Yes, for he is not subject to the necessity of nature, nor is he a slave to the order of craftsmanship. God's will is the maker and craftsman of nature, of craft and of all that exists. "And the earth was invisible and unformed." Why did he bring the heaven forth already finished, while Moses says that he shaped the earth little by little? So that, having learned his power from the better element, you might be fully assured that he could have brought this one forth finished as well, like the other. But for your sake and for your salvation he did not do so. "How was it for my sake and for my salvation?" you ask. The earth is the common table, homeland, nurse and mother of all, and our common city and tomb. Our bodies come from it, the food for our bodies comes from there, we dwell and spend our lives on it, and after death we return to it again. So, lest the urgency of your need lead you to admire it beyond its worth, and the multitude of its benefits trip you up into impiety, he shows it to you before it was completed, formless and unshaped. Seeing its weakness, you will marvel at the one who brought it forth and placed all this power in it, and you will glorify the one who prepared so many things for our ease. And God is glorified not only through correct doctrines but also through an excellent way of life. For he says, "Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." 4. I wanted to add something about almsgiving. But it seems superfluous for me to teach you by words when there now sits among us one who can instruct you by deeds: our common father and teacher. He received his ancestral house from his forebears as though for this very purpose, to give it over to the care of strangers. So he has thrown it open continually to those driven from every quarter for the sake of the truth, and he receives them and cares for them in every kind of way. I do not know, then, whether his house should be called his rather than the strangers'. Or rather, it should be considered his precisely because it belongs to the strangers. For our possessions become truly ours above all when, not for ourselves, but… [Notes: Reg. reads τεχνιτεύειν. [?] … [?] it sprouts, and neither drought. Reg. reads "two denarii", and soon after "he cast these down".]

…of the presiding clergy and on your [prayers] we cast everything, and stripped for the stadium. The prayer of the Church is so powerful that even if we were more speechless than stones, it would make our tongue lighter than any feather. When a west wind falls full on a ship's sails, it sends the vessel on swifter than an arrow. In the same way, when the prayer of the Church falls on the speaker's tongue, it sends the discourse on more forcefully than the west wind. That is why we strip for the contest every day with confidence. In outside contests, a man who has only ten or twenty admirers in so great a crowd still goes down eagerly into the contest. Much more, then, shall we do this with confidence, when not ten or twenty only but the whole theater is made up of brothers and fathers. And yet in outside contests the contestant gains nothing much from the spectator. The spectator can shout, admire what is done, and argue with those who disagree, while he sits up above. But he is not permitted to come down into the stadium, lend a hand, pull the opponent's foot or do anything of that kind. Those who first organized those contests fixed sharp stakes and ran ropes all around, and in this way they hold back the frenzy of the spectators. And what wonder is it that a spectator may not come down, when they even seat the trainer outside by the dust and tell him to give the contestants the help of his instruction from a distance, without letting him come near? But here it is not so. Both teacher and spectator may come down to us, stand close to us in spirit, and strengthen our power through their prayers. Come, then, let us take hold of the holds just as those athletes do. When they have gripped each other around the waist, the force of their holds sometimes pushes them out toward the crowd standing around, because the space is narrow. Then they release their holds and return to the place of the contest. On their return they do not grapple again standing upright, but put themselves back in the same grip they were in when they broke apart. Since the narrowness of the occasion has forced us too to break off our discourse, come, let us return to the place of the contest and take up the holds again from what was read to us today. "And God said," it says, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." This is the first thing worth asking: why was "Let us make" never said when the heaven came into being, but rather "Let there be heaven," "Let there be light," and so on for each part of creation, while here alone "Let us make" is added? Why [?] deliberation, consideration and consultation with another of equal honor? Who, then, is this one about to be made, that he enjoys such honor? It is man, the great and wonderful living being, more precious to God than all creation. For his sake heaven and earth and sea and all the rest of the body of creation [were made]. It is man, whose salvation God so longed for that he did not spare even his Only-begotten for his sake. For he did not stop doing and working at everything until he had brought him up and seated [?] … to create, nor of archangels. [Note: What is missing in Morel.]

…[make] man? The Wonderful Counsellor, the one who holds authority, the mighty God, the Prince of peace, the Father of the age to come: the only-begotten Son of God himself. It is to him, then, that he says, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." He did not say "mine and yours," or "mine and all of yours," but "according to our image," showing that the image is one and the likeness is one. But God and the angels do not share one image or one likeness. How could the Master and his ministers have one image and likeness? So your argument is refuted on every side. What he indicated here is an image of rule, as what follows shows. Having said "according to image and likeness," he added, "and let them rule over the fish of the sea." But God and the angels could not share one rule. How could slaves share the rule of their Master, or ministers the rule of the one who commands them? But again, others attack us and say that God has the same kind of image that we have. They misunderstand what was said. He did not speak of an image of substance but of an image of rule, as we shall show from what follows. To see that the Divine does not have human form, hear Paul saying, "For a man ought not to cover himself, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man. Therefore," he says, "she ought to have a covering on her head." Now if he used the word "image" here to indicate an exact likeness of form to God, and man is called the image of God because God is shaped like this, then by their reasoning not only the man but also the woman should be called the image. For man and woman share one form and one stamp, and the likeness is one. Why, then, is the man called the image of God, but not the woman? Because he does not mean an image in form but an image in rule. The man alone has this, and the woman does not. He is subject to no one, while she has been placed under him, as God says: "Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you." So the man is the image of God, since he has no one above him, just as no one is above God, and he rules over all. The woman is the glory of the man, since she is subject to the man. And again elsewhere he says that we ought not to think the Divine is like gold or silver or stone, or anything engraved by human art or imagination. What he means is this: the Divine surpasses not only visible shapes, but even the mind could not picture what God is like. How, then, could God have a human form, when Paul says that there is no mind at all able to form an image of God's substance within itself? For any of us could easily picture our own form and shape in our thoughts. Again I wanted to add something about almsgiving now as well, but time does not allow us. So let us now fall silent, urging you to hold fast to everything that has been said, and to take great care for right living, so that not… [Notes: Reg. reads "to cover the head". Reg. reads "has risen above". Reg. reads "what is desired".]

…there is no need to be carried down into the dark depths of the abyss, or to entrust the body's safety to the rush of senseless waters. Here there is abundant light, brighter than the sun's rays themselves, great calm and no turmoil at all, and what we find here is so profitable that words cannot even describe it. So let us not grow weary, but take up the inquiry. You heard that God made man according to the image of God. We have already said what this "according to the image" and "according to the likeness" mean. "According to the image" is not identity of substance but likeness of rule. "According to the likeness" means being gentle and meek, and becoming like God, as far as we can, in virtue. As Christ says, "Become like my Father who is in heaven." On this broad and spacious earth, some animals are more brutish and others more savage. In the same way, in the breadth of our soul, some thoughts are more brutish, like cattle, and others more savage and wild. We must master them, overcome them, and hand over the rule of them to reason. "And how could anyone overcome a savage thought?" someone asks. What are you saying, man? We overcome lions and tame their souls, and you doubt whether you can turn the savagery of a thought into gentleness? Yet for the lion wildness is natural and gentleness unnatural, while for you it is the opposite: gentleness is natural and savagery unnatural. You drive out what is natural from the soul of a beast and implant what is unnatural, and you cannot preserve what is natural in your own soul? What great negligence that would be! And with the souls of lions there is a further difficulty besides, for the beast's soul has no reason. Yet you have often seen lions tamer than sheep being led through the marketplace, and many people in the workshops have often paid money to the keeper as a reward for the skill and wisdom by which he tamed the beast. But in the human soul there is reason, and the fear of God, and much help from many sides. So do not give me excuses and pretexts. If you are willing, you can be gentle and meek. "Let us make man according to our image and likeness, and let them rule over the beasts." 2. Here the Greeks attack us and say that this saying is false. "We do not rule the beasts," they say. "They rule us and cause us great distress." For the most part, this is not true. The mere sight of a human face is enough to make a beast flee, so great is their fear of us. And if one does sometimes attack in self-defense, compelled by hunger, or because we have often hemmed them in and driven them to it, that would not then [count against] complete rule. For if one of us saw robbers coming, armed himself and went to defend himself, that would not be a matter of rule either, but of [?]… [Notes: Reg. reads "not likeness of substance, but the dignity of rule". [?] the soul is devoid of reason. [?] being called. Patrologia Graeca 54.]

[?] we may lay down. He left the various kinds of beasts of burden, so that they might share our labors in carrying our loads; he left flocks of sheep, so that we might have enough to clothe ourselves; and he allowed other kinds of animals as well, which bring us many other uses. For since, when he was punishing man, he said, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” he lightened the heavy and burdensome sweat with the multitude of irrational animals that share this labor and hardship with us, so that this sweat and toil and labor might not be unbearable. And just as a kind and caring master who has flogged his own servant applies some treatment to the stripes, so too God, having imposed a sentence, wishes in every way to make this sentence lighter. He condemned us to sweat and continual labor, but he provided many kinds of irrational animals to share the labor with us. For all these things, then, let us give him thanks. For his giving us the honor, and his taking the honor away again, and his not taking all of it away, and his setting the fear of wild beasts over us: all of these, if one examines them, are full of great wisdom, great care, and great love for humankind. May we all enjoy that love continually, to the glory of God who has done these things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

That sin introduced three kinds of servitude; and against those who listen carelessly, and those who do not honor their parents. 1. Yesterday you heard how God made man king and ruler of the wild beasts, and how he immediately cast him out of the kingship. Or rather, it was not God who cast him out, but man cast himself out of the honor through his disobedience. For his obtaining the kingship came about through God’s love for humankind alone. God did not give him this as a reward for good deeds; rather, he adorned him with the honor even before he came into being. So that you may not say that man came into being and then, after many good deeds, drew God to give him rule over the beasts, God speaks of his rule when he is about to fashion him, saying, “Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness, and let them rule over the wild beasts of the earth.” The honor came before life, the crown before creation, and before he came into being he was raised to the royal throne. Men honor those under them only in extreme old age, after many labors and countless dangers, in peace and in war. God does not act so; he brought man to this honor as soon as he came into being, showing that what happened was not a reward for good deeds but divine grace, and not something owed. His receiving the rule, then, came about through God’s love for humankind alone; but his falling from the rule came from his own negligence. For just as kings remove from office those who do not obey their commands, so God did with man, and then removed him from his rule. It is necessary today to say how much other honor the nature of sin took away, and how many kinds of servitude it introduced [?]. [Variant readings: one Regius manuscript reads “but his being cast out of rule”; the same reads “to a woman.”]

For she once exercised authority badly. “But to be in quietness.” But tell us the reason too. “For Adam,” he says, “was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression.” That is why he brought her down from the teacher’s chair. Whoever does not know how to teach, he says, should learn. But if he does not wish to learn and wants to teach instead, he will destroy both himself and those who learn from him, which is just what happened with the woman then. That she is subject to the man, and was made subject because of sin, is clear from this. But I want to hear that other saying: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” 2. I want to learn how Paul too speaks of this care, and mixes mastery with tender affection. Where, then, does he do this? Writing to the Corinthians, he says, “Husbands, love your wives.” There you have “Your turning shall be toward your husband.” “Wives, that they fear their husbands.” There you have “He shall rule over you.” Do you see how light the mastery is, when the master is passionately in love with the one who serves, when fear is joined with love? This is how the burden of servitude is removed. Disobedience, then, introduced one form of rule. Do not look at the fact that God set it in proper order, but at the fact that sin created the very nature of servitude. There is also a second kind of servitude, heavier than the first, and it too has its origin and occasion in sin. After the flood in the time of Noah, after the common shipwreck of the whole world and that total destruction, Ham sinned against his father. Seeing his father naked, he stripped him still more by denouncing him to his brothers, and from then on he became a servant of his brothers. The wickedness of his choice spoiled the nobility of his nature, and quite rightly. Scripture puts together countless defenses on behalf of the righteous man; or rather, with one word it grants him complete pardon. “Noah,” it says, “began to be a farmer.” This “began” provides a strong defense of his drunkenness. He did not know how much wine one ought to drink, nor how to drink it, whether undiluted or mixed with water, nor when to drink it, whether as soon as it was drawn from the vats or after waiting a little while. Scripture, then, defends Noah in these ways. But the one born from him, the one saved through him (for it was because of the honor shown to his father that he did not perish with the rest in the deluge), took no account of nature itself, did not remember his rescue, and was not sobered by fear. Though he still saw the remnants of God’s wrath remaining, the traces of the disaster still visible, and the fear of what had happened still at its height, he insulted his father. That is why a wise man advises, “Do not glorify yourself in your father’s dishonor, for your father’s dishonor is no glory to you.” But Ham did not know even this; he committed a sin beyond all pardon and defense. Therefore he paid servitude as the penalty for his sin, became a servant of his brothers, and the [?] from the [?] [Variant reading: the first Regius manuscript, today 779, reads “and mixes tender affection with mastery.”]

3. How then does Paul say, “There is no authority except from God”? Because God himself established it for our benefit. Sin introduced the need for it, but God used it for our good. Just as the need for medicines arises from wounds, while the applying of medicines comes from the skill of physicians, so too the need for servitude arose from sin, while setting it in proper order came from the wisdom of God. But rouse yourselves and put away your sluggishness. Why do I say this? We are expounding the Scriptures to you, but you have turned your eyes away from us to the lamps and to the man who is lighting them. What negligence it is to leave us and pay attention to him! I too am lighting a fire, the fire from the Scriptures, and on our tongue burns the lamp of teaching. This light is greater and better than that one. We do not light a wick soaked in oil, as he does; we kindle souls watered with piety with the desire to listen. Paul too once preached in an upper room. Let no one think that I am comparing myself with Paul; I am not so mad. I say it so that you may learn how much zeal you should show in listening. Paul, then, was preaching in an upper room, and evening came on, as it has now, and there were lamps in the upper room. Then Eutychus fell from the window, yet the fall did not break up the gathering, nor did the death make the audience get up. They were so riveted to hearing the divine oracles that they did not even notice the fall. But you, though you see nothing strange or remarkable, only a man doing his usual work, have turned your gaze over there. What pardon could this deserve? So let no one, beloved, think this rebuke burdensome. We reproach you not out of hatred but out of care. “For the wounds of friends are more trustworthy than the willing kisses of enemies.” Rouse yourselves, then, I beg you, and leave that fire and attend to the light of the divine Scriptures. For I want to tell you of another kind of rule, one that takes its occasion not from sin but from nature itself. What is it? The rule of parents over their children. Such honor is a repayment for the pangs of birth. That is why a wise man says, “Serve those who begot you as masters.” Then he adds the reason, saying, “For what will you give back to them, as they have given to you?” And yet what is there that a child cannot repay a father? He means nothing other than this: as they begot you, you will never be able to beget them. Since, then, we fall short in this respect, let us make it up in another by the honors we pay them, not only because of the law of nature, but, even before nature, because of the fear of God. For God earnestly wishes parents to be honored by their children. Those who do this he rewards with great blessings and gifts, while those who transgress this law he punishes with great and terrible evils. “Whoever speaks evil of father or mother,” he says, “shall die the death [?]” [Variant reading: one Regius manuscript reads “I light a fire below.”]

That we are not punished because of Adam, and that the good things are greater than the grievous things brought in through him, if we pay attention to ourselves; and against those who pass by the poor. 1. Perhaps you think that we have completed the whole discourse on mastery, but I still see much fruit appearing in it. Do not grow weary, I beg you, until we have harvested all of it. When hard-working farmers see a vine luxuriant with leaves and heavy with fruit, they do not cut only the outer clusters; they go further in, bending back the shoots and lifting the leaves, so that not even the grapes of a small bunch hidden under the foliage escape them. Do not show yourselves lazier than they are, then, and do not leave until you have received it all, especially since the labor is mine and the fruit is yours. Yesterday we accused women, or rather not women but Eve, of introducing servitude through sin. Women might say to us, “Why then, when she sinned, were we condemned? The fault was one person’s, yet the charge falls on the whole of human nature.” Slaves too might say, “Why on earth, when Canaan insulted his father, did the punishment pass on to the whole race?” And those who fear rulers might raise the same complaint: “Why on earth, when others lived in wickedness, were we handed over to the yoke of rule?” What then shall we say to all of these? There will be one answer to all the questions: the first people sinned and through their own disobedience introduced servitude, and once it had been introduced, those who came after confirmed it by their own sins. If they could show that they had always been pure of sin, perhaps they might seem to have good grounds to object. But if they too are liable to many penalties, this defense is pointless. For I did not say that this sin brings in servitude and another does not [?], but that every sin has servitude as its lot; I blamed the nature of sin, not only a particular kind of sin. Just as all incurable diseases lead to death, though not all are of the same nature, so all sins give birth to servitude, though not all are of the same nature. Eve sinned by touching the tree and was condemned for it. So do not you in turn commit another sin, perhaps more grievous than hers. The same is worth saying of slaves and of subjects: the first people introduced sin, but those who succeeded them kept the power of mastery in force through their own offenses. I can also answer in another way: many who returned to virtue were freed from mastery. First, if you like, let us test the argument on the women, so that you may see how blessed Paul, who put the chains on them, himself loosed them again. “If any woman,” he says, “has an unbelieving husband [?] … you do not serve my gods, and the

golden image which I set up, you do not worship?” What then did they say? See how virtue made them, though captives, more kingly than the king, and showed their spirit to be loftier than his. They answered with boldness, not as men speaking to a king, but as if addressing a subject. “We have no need,” they say, “to answer the king concerning this matter.” We will give our proof not by words but by deeds. “There is a God in heaven able to deliver us.” They reminded him of the kindness shown in Daniel’s case, using the very words the prophet had spoken then. What did Daniel say? “The matter the king demands is not for magi, Gazarenes, or Chaldeans; but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.” They remind him of this saying in order to make him more lenient. Then they say, “And if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image you set up.” See the wisdom of those young men. So that those present would not accuse God of weakness if it should happen that they fell into the furnace and died, they confessed his power beforehand, saying, “There is a God in heaven who is able to deliver us.” And again, so that if they escaped the flame they would not be thought to serve God for pay and reward, they added, “And if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image you set up.” In this way they at once proclaimed the power of God and displayed the steadfastness of their own souls, so that no one could say of them what the devil said slanderously about Job. What did the devil say about Job? “Does Job worship you for nothing? For you have fenced in everything inside and outside him.” So that no one could say this about them too, they stopped that shameless mouth in advance. But, as I was saying, even if someone is a captive, a slave, or a foreigner, even if he lives in a strange land, as long as he has virtue with him he will be more kingly than all kings. Have you seen the servitude of women loosed, and that of slaves, and that of subjects? Come, I will now show you the fear of wild beasts cast out as well. Once, in that same Babylon, they threw Daniel into the pit, but the lions did not dare touch him. For they saw the ancient royal image shining in him; they saw those features which they had seen in Adam before sin. It was with the same submission that they came to Adam then and received their names. And this happened not only here but also with blessed Paul. Cast up on the island of the barbarians, he sat by a fire warming himself; then a viper leapt out of the brushwood and fastened on his hand. What happened next? The creature fell off at once. Since it found no sin, it could not even bite. Just as we, when we try to climb a smooth rock and find no handhold anywhere, fall at once, even if sea or chasm lies below, so too that creature, even with a fire lying below, found no handhold of sin, nor where [?]

[?] seeing people, we hurry home in this way. “Hunger compels me,” someone says. Then let hunger persuade you to stay. As the proverb says, full stomachs do not know hungry ones, while hungry ones recognize another’s need from their own; or rather, not even so is it possible to perceive it fully. You run to a table already prepared and cannot bear to wait even a little; but the poor man stands there until evening itself, hurrying and straining to scrape together his daily food. And when he sees the day over and the money, enough for one day’s food, not yet complete, he is pained and burns inside, and is forced to venture beyond his own strength. That is why in the evening they press upon us more vehemently, swearing, adjuring, lamenting, wailing, stretching out their hands, forced into countless other kinds of shamelessness. For they fear that, once everyone has left, they will be left wandering in the city as in a desert. Those who are shipwrecked by day, once they have seized a plank, hurry to reach the harbor before evening, lest night come on while they are still out and they suffer a worse shipwreck. In the same way the poor, fearing hunger as they would a shipwreck, hurry to gather enough money for food before evening, so that they will not be left outside the harbor when everyone has gone home. For their harbor is the hands of those who help them. 4. But we are moved by their misfortunes neither in the marketplace nor when we have gone home. Even with our table set before us, often full of countless good things (if we should call good what we eat to the condemnation of our inhumanity), even with the table set, we hear them below walking through the alleys and crying aloud in the streets, grieving in the deepest darkness and in great desolation, and still we are not moved. Even when we have eaten our fill and are going to bed, and hear them again at that hour lamenting loudly below, we pass it by as though we were hearing a mad dog and not a human voice. We pay no attention to the hour, that late at night, when everyone is asleep, he alone is lamenting; nor to how small the request is, that he asks us for nothing more than bread or a little money; nor to the greatness of his misfortune, that he wrestles with unending hunger; nor to the modesty of the suppliant, that though gripped by such need he does not dare to come to the door or draw near, but makes his plea from below, from a great distance. If he receives something, he offers countless prayers; if he does not, even then he utters no bitter word, nor does he revile and curse those who could give and do not. Instead, like someone being led by an executioner to unbearable punishment, who begs all the passers-by, entreating them, and finding no help, with much

When we meet with so many brothers and fathers, and such ones, how could we not lay aside all discouragement? How could we not reap every delight? This assembly is better than the gatherings in the marketplaces not only in its size but in the very nature of its conversation. People who meet in the marketplaces and sit together in a circle often talk about useless things, bring up dull topics, and speak about matters that are no concern of theirs. For as a rule we are more eager to pry into other people's affairs and meddle in them. I pass over for now the fact that it is risky and dangerous to utter and to hear such words and be carried away by them, and that storms have often been stirred up in households by such gatherings. But no one would deny that all that talk is useless, dull and worldly, and that a spiritual word would hardly ever find its way into such an assembly. Here it is not so; it is quite the opposite. All unprofitable talk has been driven out, and all spiritual teaching has been brought in. We talk about our soul and the goods that belong to the soul; about the crowns stored up in heaven; about lives of distinction; about God's love for humankind and his providence over all things; and about everything else that concerns us most closely: why we were made, what lot will meet us after our departure from here, and how things will stand with us then. And it is not we alone who share in this assembly; prophets and apostles share in it too. Greatest of all, the Master of all things himself, Jesus, stands in our midst. For he says, "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst." If he is in their midst where two or three are gathered, much more is he present in the midst where there are so many men, so many women, so many fathers, together with apostles and prophets. That is why we too speak with greater eagerness, enjoying the help that comes from there, and we now make good our promise to you. We promised to speak first about the tree: whether Adam's knowledge of good and evil came from it, or whether he had this discernment even before he ate. We can now say confidently that he had this discernment even before eating. For if he did not know what is good and what is evil, he would have been more irrational than the irrational animals, and the master would have been more foolish than his servants. Would it not be absurd that goats and sheep know which plant is useful to them and which is deadly, and do not go after everything that comes into view, but have discernment and know clearly what harms them and what helps them, while man should be deprived of such security? If he did not have this, he would be worth nothing; he would be more worthless than everything else. [Note:] Reg. reads "we shall render to you."

Why it is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil [?], and what it is; and on "Today you will be with me in paradise." 1. Yesterday I urged your love again and again to remember what had been said, and to set out a double [table] in the evening [?] [Patrologia Graeca 54]

the matter required. But when the Master commands us even to increase them, consider how much labor and care we need, we to whom they have been entrusted. That is why the one who was entrusted with five talents brought back not only what he had been given but as many again. The talents were the gift of his master's kindness, but the servant also had to show his own diligence. Likewise the one entrusted with two talents earned two more, and for this he was counted worthy of the same honor by his master. But another, entrusted with one talent, brought back exactly what he had been given. He did not reduce or diminish the deposit, nor return only half of it; yet because he did not put it to work and did not bring back double what had been entrusted to him, he paid the ultimate penalty, and quite rightly. "If I had wanted them only to be kept safe," the master says, "and no further trading to be done with them, I would not have put them into my servants' hands." But notice the master's kindness. The one entrusted with five talents brought five more, and the one with two brought as many again, and each received the same reward. Just as he said to the first, "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much," so he says to the one who brought two, "Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much." The return was not the same, yet the wage was the same; so he counted this one worthy of the same honor too. Why? Because God looked not at the amount brought back but at the ability of those who worked. Each of them did what he was able to do. The greater and smaller amounts brought back were due not to the laziness of the one or the diligence of the other, but to the difference in what was deposited with them. One received five and brought five more; the other received two and brought two, and fell short in nothing as far as diligence goes. Both this one and that one doubled what had been entrusted to them. But the one who received one talent brought back only the single talent, and so he was punished. 2. You have heard, then, how great a punishment awaits those who do not trade with the Master's money. Let us therefore guard it, trade with it, and carry on a busy commerce with it. Let no one say, "I am a layman, I am a learner, I have no skill in teaching; I am uneducated and worth nothing." Even if you are a layman, even if you are uneducated, even if you have been entrusted with one talent, work with what has been put into your hands, and you will receive the same wage as the teacher. I am fully convinced that you are keeping what has been said and holding on to it with great care. But so that we do not spend the whole sermon on this, come, let us add for your love what follows from what we said yesterday, giving you this as the reward for keeping it. For one who has been entrusted with the earlier things and has kept them deserves to receive more. What, then, was the account set before us yesterday? We were speaking about the tree, and we showed that man knew good and evil before he ate from the tree, and that he was filled with great wisdom. This is clear from his giving names to the animals, from his recognizing his own wife, and from his saying, "This now is bone of my

for when God said, "Where is Abel your brother?" he said, "Am I my brother's keeper?" From this it is plain that he set about this deed knowing clearly what he was doing. Just as Cain knew even before the experience that murder is evil, but learned it more clearly afterwards, when he received his punishment and heard, "You shall be groaning and trembling on the earth," so too his father had the knowledge of good and evil even before he ate, though not as clearly as after eating from the tree. Why do I say this? Because we all know evil things even before we do them, but we learn them more clearly after we have done them, and much more clearly when we are punished. So Cain also knew even before the deed that killing his brother was evil, but afterwards he learned it more clearly through his punishment. In the same way we know, even before experiencing it, that health is good and sickness is evil; but much more, when we fall sick, [do we learn] the difference between the two

3. In the same way Adam too knew that obedience is good and disobedience is evil, but he learned it more clearly later, when he tasted of the tree, was cast out of paradise and fell from that blessedness. Since he fell into punishment because he tasted of the tree when God had forbidden it, the punishment taught him more clearly, through experience, how evil it is to disobey God and how good it is to obey. That is why it is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And why, if the tree did not by its own nature hold the knowledge of good and evil, and man learned this more clearly from the punishment for his disobedience regarding the tree, is it called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil? Because it is Scripture's custom, when something happens in a certain place or at a certain time, to name the places and the times after what happened. To make this clearer, I will show it to you by examples. Isaac once dug wells. His neighbors tried to spoil these wells, and enmity arose from it, and he called the well "Enmity": not because the well itself was hostile, but because the enmity arose over it. So too the tree is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because it had knowledge itself, but because the test of the knowledge of good and evil took place over it. Again, Abraham dug a well; Abimelech plotted against him; they came together, put an end to their enmity, swore oaths to each other, and called that well "the Well of the Oath": not because the well swore, but because the oath was made over the well. Do you see how places are not the causes of events, even though they take their names from events? We really must bring forward examples, so that what is being said becomes clearer. Again, Jacob saw angels coming to meet him and the camp of God, and he called the place "Camp." Yet the place was not the camp; still the place was called "Camp" because he saw the camp there. Do you see how he named the place after what happened in it? So too the tree is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because it had the knowledge of good and evil itself, but because the proof of the knowledge of good and evil took place over it, and the testing of disobedience and obedience. [?] ...of all, and before the apostles, so that none of those

who came after should despair of entering, or give up hope of his own salvation, when he sees the man who was full of countless evils dwelling in the royal courts. But let us see whether the thief showed any labors, achievements and fruits. No, that cannot be said. By a bare word, by faith alone, he leapt into paradise ahead of the apostles, so that you may learn that it was not so much his good disposition that prevailed, but the Master's love for humankind that did it all. For what did the thief say? What did he do? Did he fast? Did he weep? Did he tear his clothes? Did he show repentance over a long time? Not at all. On the cross itself, after the sentence had been passed, he obtained salvation. See the speed: from the cross to heaven, from condemnation to salvation. What, then, were those words? What power did they have, that they won him such great goods? "Remember me," he says, "in your kingdom." And what is this? He asked to receive good things; he showed no diligence in works. But the one who knew his heart paid attention not to his words but to the disposition of his mind. Those who had enjoyed the teachings of the prophets, who had seen the signs and witnessed the miracles, said of Christ, "He has a demon," and, "He leads the crowd astray." But the thief, who had not heard the prophets or seen miracles, saw him nailed to the cross and paid no attention to the disgrace or the dishonor; he looked to the Godhead itself and said, "Remember me in your kingdom." This is new and astonishing. You see a cross, and you remember a kingdom? What did you see that was worthy of a kingdom? A crucified man, struck, mocked, accused, spat upon, scourged. Tell me, are these things worthy of a kingdom? Do you see that he looked with the eyes of faith and did not judge by what appeared? That is why God, for his part, did not weigh his bare words; but just as the thief looked to the Godhead, so God looked into the thief's heart and said, "Today you will be with me in paradise." Pay attention here, for no small question arises. The Manichaeans, those dogs, mindless and raving, put on an outward show of gentleness but have within them the savage madness of dogs, and they hide the wolf under the sheep's skin. Do not look at what appears; examine the beast hidden within. These people seize on this passage and say: "Christ said, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.' So the repayment of the good things has already taken place, and the resurrection is superfluous. For if the thief received the good things on that day, while his body has not yet risen even today, there will be no resurrection of bodies at all." Have you grasped what was said, or must I say it a second time? "Truly, truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." "So the thief," they say, "entered paradise without his body. How could he have entered with it, when his body had not been buried, nor had it decayed and become dust? And nowhere is it said that Christ raised him. If he brought the thief in, and the thief enjoyed the good things without his body, it is evident that there is no resurrection of the body. For if there were a resurrection of the body, he would not have said, 'Today you will be with me in paradise,' but, 'at the time of the consummation, when the resurrection of bodies takes place.'" But if he has already brought in the [?] ... unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he

cannot enter the kingdom of heaven." If then he promised the kingdom of heaven but brought the thief into paradise, he has not yet given him the good things. But they reply to this with another argument. "By paradise here," they say, "he did not mean paradise; he called the kingdom of heaven by the name of paradise. Since he was speaking with a thief, a man who had heard nothing of the lofty doctrines and knew nothing of prophecy, but had spent all his time in deserted places committing murders, who had never so much as peeped into a church or shared in hearing the divine word, and did not know what the kingdom of heaven is, he said to him, 'Today you will be with me in paradise.' By the better-known and more familiar name of paradise Christ indicates the kingdom of heaven, and it is about that kingdom that he speaks to him." I accept this. "So," he says, "the thief entered the kingdom of heaven." How is that clear? "From his saying, 'Today you will be with me in paradise.'" If this solution seems rather forced, we will bring in a clearer one. What is it? Christ said, "Whoever does not believe in the Son has already been judged." What then? Has he already been judged? Yet there is no resurrection yet, no chastisement and punishment yet; how then has he already been judged? By reason of his sin. And again he says, "Whoever believes in the Son has passed from death into life." He did not say "will pass" but "has already passed": the one by reason of his good deed, the other by reason of his sin. So just as the one has been judged though not yet judged, and the other has passed into life though not yet having passed, and he speaks to the one on the basis of his good deed and to the other on the basis of his sin, of things not yet done as if they had already happened, so too he spoke to the thief. Doctors, too, when they see someone whose case is hopeless, say that he has already died and is a dead man, even though they see him still breathing. Just as that patient, since he has no hope of recovery, is dead in the eyes of the doctors, so too the thief, since there was no longer any prospect of his turning back to destruction, has entered heaven. So too Adam heard, "On the day you eat from the tree, you shall surely die." What then? Did he die on that very day? Not at all; he lived nine hundred years and more after that day. How then did God say, "On that very day you shall die"? By the sentence, not by the experience. In this way the thief too entered heaven. Listen, then, to what Paul says, showing that no one has yet received the repayment of the good things. Speaking of the prophets and the righteous, he added: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and greeted them, since God had foreseen something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us." Hold on to these things, remember them, and teach those who have not heard them; let each of you meditate on them in church, in the marketplace and at home. For nothing is sweeter than hearing the divine word. Listen, then, to what he says about th[?] ... battle. That is why we too, with confidence, the word

we put forward for teaching, casting the whole matter on their prayers. To make the hearing easier and clearer for you, let us briefly remind you of what was said to you yesterday. I said that man knew good and evil before eating from the tree, and that he did not receive this knowledge after tasting it. I said why it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and how it is Scripture's custom, when something happens in a certain place or at a certain time, to name both the place and the time after the event. Today we must read the commandment itself by which he forbade eating from the tree. What is it? "And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying, 'From every tree that is in paradise you may freely eat.'" The law is divine; let us pay attention. If, when people read out imperial letters, they make the whole theater stand up, how much more ought we, who are about to read the laws not of men but of God, to rise up in our minds and attend to the

I know that some people accuse the lawgiver and say that the law is the cause of the transgression. So we must first take a stand against this and show from the facts themselves that he gave the law not because he hated man or wanted to insult our nature, but because he loved us and cared for us. That he gave it as an ally to us, hear what Isaiah says: "For he gave the law as a help." One who hates does not help. Again the Prophet cries out, "Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." One who hates does not dispel darkness with a lamp, nor guide the one who has gone astray with light. Again Solomon says, "The commandment of the law is a lamp and a light, and life, and reproof and instruction." See, it is not only a help, not only a lamp, but also light and life. These are not the acts of one who hates or wants to destroy, but of one who stretches out a hand and lifts up. That is why Paul too, addressing the Jew and showing how much profit the law brought and that it is a relief to our nature, not a burden, said, "But if you call yourself a Jew and rest upon the law." Do you see that God gave the law not to burden our nature but to give it rest? Do you want to learn that he gave it to honor us as well? These things are indeed quite enough to show his honor and care; still, I will make the same point plain from other testimonies as well. "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem," he says; "praise your God, O Zion; for he has strengthened the bars of your gates, he has blessed your children within you; he makes your borders peace and fills you with the finest of wheat." Then, after speaking of the benefits God supplies through the rest of creation, he added the special and greater one, speaking thus: "He sends his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so for any other nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them." See how many good things he listed. The safety of the city: for "he has strengthened the bars of your gates," he says. Deliverance from wars: for "he makes your borders peace," he says.

not only boasting in the reconciliation, but also in having received the reconciliation through Christ? And again, extolling the resurrection, he says, "The Lord himself will descend from heaven." See how there too everything is done through the Master. So here too, it was not through some servant, not through an angel or archangel, but he himself in person gave the command to Adam, honoring man with a double honor: by giving the law, and by giving it himself. How, then, did Adam slip? Through his own negligence. This is shown by all who received a law and did not slip, but even did more than was commanded. But since I see that the time is pressing us, I will put off the discussion to another sermon. Meanwhile, keep what has been said and remember it, and teach those who have not heard it; let each of you meditate on these things in church, in the marketplace and at home. For nothing is sweeter than hearing the divine word. Listen, then, to what the Prophet says about it: "How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth." So set this honeycomb on your evening table, to fill the whole meal with spiritual delight. Do you not see how the wealthy bring in lyre-players and flute-players after dinner? They make their own house a theater; you make your house a heaven. You will do this not by changing the walls or altering the foundations, but by inviting the Master of heaven himself to your table. Do you not

On [?] ... how [?] ... the sins of the brothers [?] ... and that [?] ... was said, and on [?] of Noah; that it was not by chance that the righteous received their names, but by God's dispensation. 1. If it were possible for you to know what has been said by us and what remains, and where we [broke off] the discourse

[?] …the memory of these things will [?], as they are reminded once again of what they heard. And those who were absent, not through [?] but because of some devilish circumstance, will suffer no harm, since the discourse makes the teaching more familiar to them by going back to the beginning. Now perhaps those of you who are always present might say that for this very reason I should not have taken up again what had already been said: those who were absent and despised the assemblies should feel the loss in fact, and so become better, disciplined by the penalty. I praise you for being so stung by your brothers' negligence, and I admire your zeal; but I want you to temper this zeal with kindness as well. For zeal stripped of forgiveness is not zeal but rather anger, and an admonition that lacks kindness looks like a kind of spite. That is why I urge you instead not to judge your neighbors' sins harshly. Whoever looks at his brothers' wounds without forgiveness will find no one to grant him forgiveness if he himself should ever sin. In the same way, whoever judges his neighbors' faults with mercy will see many stretching out a hand to him if he is ever tripped up. I say this now not because I want to increase the negligence of those who were absent, but because I am eager to make our care for them more intense, so that it may be carried out with reason and with affection. For we too, the day before, spoke at great length against them, and even said they were not human beings, as you remember. We set over them as accusers two of the foremost prophets. One says, “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one to answer.” The other cries out again and asks, “To whom shall I speak and bear witness? Their ears are uncircumcised, and they cannot hear.” With these words and others like them we stung their minds sharply. But now we exhort them again, for this is what Paul commanded: “Reprove,” he says, “rebuke, exhort.” One must not always do only the one thing, or only the other, but mix the two and so produce a complete benefit. If we reprove all the time, we make them more shameless; if we exhort all the time, we make them more careless. That is why physicians do not only cut but also bind up wounds. Nor do they always apply bitter medicines; often they apply gentle ones too. With the first they clean away what has rotted, and with the second they soothe the pain the first has caused. That is why Paul also says elsewhere: “Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, restore such a one, looking to yourself, lest you too be tempted.” Excellent advice, perfect counsel, full of care and showing a father's tender heart: truly, brothers, these words are worthy of Paul's tongue. At once, with the name of kinship, he drew the hearer toward goodwill. You were born of the same birth pangs as he was, you were raised on the same food, you had the same father, you shared with him in the spiritual birth. Show this kinship, then, in correcting his falls as well. “If he is overtaken.” He did not say, “If he sins,” but turned to a kind of sin that admits of forgiveness. For “if he is overtaken” means if he is set upon, if he is deceived; not the one who from deliberate…

…looking to [?] propriety, [they do not] disregard the misfortune of those others. Instead they stop the ship, let down the anchors and take in the sails, and they throw out ropes and cast planks into the sea, so that the man about to be swamped by the waves may grab one of them and escape the shipwreck. Imitate the sailors, then, O man. For you too are sailing a great and wide sea, the length of this present life. It is a sea with wild beasts and pirates, a sea with reefs and rocks, a sea stirred up by many waves and storms, and many people often suffer shipwreck on this sea too. So when you see one of your fellow travelers who has lost the wealth of salvation through some devilish circumstance, tossed by the waves and about to go under, stop your ship. Even if you are hurrying somewhere else, set your own affairs aside and see to his rescue. For the man about to sink cannot bear delay or slowness. So go to him quickly, snatch him swiftly from the surge, and pull every rope to haul him up from the depths of destruction. Even if countless affairs pull you away, let nothing be more urgent than rescuing the one in distress, for if you choose to put it off even a little, you will abandon him to the fury of the storm. In such calamities, then, we need speed: speed and intense earnestness. Hear how Paul hurries, and rouses many others, when he sees a man about to sink: “Confirm your love toward him,” he says, “lest such a one be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.” That is why he commands them to stretch out a hand quickly, so that he is not swallowed up while we hesitate and delay. Let us be caring, then, toward our brothers. This is the chief point of our way of life, and this is its distinguishing mark: not to look to our own interests alone, but also to straighten and restore our members that have been put out of joint. This is the greatest proof of faith: “For by this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” What shows genuine love is not sharing a table, nor a mere greeting, nor flattering words. It is correcting our neighbor and looking to his benefit, raising up the fallen, and stretching out a hand to the one lying on the ground, neglecting our own safety and seeking our neighbor's good before our own. This is the mark of genuine love. For love does not look to its own interests; it sees its neighbor's before its own, so that through them it may see its own. That is why I too am now delivering such long discourses, not for my own sake but for yours. And you, then, should listen not only for your own sake but also for the sake of others, who are to be taught by you. For the body of the Church is nourished through the connection of its members. A member that keeps all the food to itself and does not share it with its neighbor both harms itself and ruins the rest of the body. So the stomach, if it alone keeps the food, [ruins] the rest of the body too [?]

…in the Syriac language means “beyond,” as those familiar with that language know. And the Syriac language is closely related to the Hebrew tongue. “And why was he called a man from beyond?” someone asks. The land of Judea, that is, the whole of Palestine from Egypt to the Euphrates, lies opposite Babylonia, where Abraham came from. The river flows between the two and forms a common boundary for both lands. Since he was not from Palestine but came from beyond, from Babylonia, he took his name from the place and from what happened, and was called a man from beyond, because he came from beyond. And why did he come from beyond? Because God commanded it. And why did God command it? To show the righteous man's obedience. And how did he show the righteous man's obedience? At God's command he left his own land and exchanged it for a foreign one. Do you see what a long chain is woven from the righteous man's title? This name has opened up for us a whole sea of history. Learn his ancient name, then. When you see him living in Palestine, his title will lead you back by the hand to his original homeland, and as you learn why he left it, you will receive encouragement enough to share the same zeal. For though he lived before the law and before life under the law, he displayed the wisdom of the age of grace. What Christ later said to the apostles, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, who will not receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life,” Abraham carried out in his deeds before grace came. And the righteous man's wisdom can be seen not only from this but also from God's promise itself: “Come,” he says, “into the land that I will show you.” Both homelands could be perceived by the senses, but one was his own and the other foreign; one was visible and the other unknown; one was in his hands and the other only in hope. Yet he left what was visible, certain and in hand, and ran toward what was unseen and uncertain, things he did not possess. He did this to persuade and teach you that when God commands you to leave what is certain and look to what is uncertain, you should not object or argue. For the things in our hands are not as certain as the things in hope, and this present life is not as certain as the life to come. This life we see with our own eyes; that one we see with the eyes of faith. This one we see lying in our hands; that one we see kept safe by God's promises. 4. And God's promises are far stronger than our hands. Do you want to learn how this present life always lies in uncertainty, while the life to come, which seems uncertain, is clearer than the present one, more secure and lasting? Let us examine, if you like, the splendid things of this present life: wealth, glory, power, the honors that come from men. You will see that nothing is more uncertain than these. What is less trustworthy than wealth, which often does not stay with us even until evening? Like an ungrateful runaway slave, it keeps passing from this man to that one, and then from that one to another. Glory is much the same. The man who was brilliant and distinguished before is suddenly without honor and without a name [?]… all, not having received the promises, but

having seen them from afar. What are you saying? Did Abraham not receive the promises? Did he not come into Palestine? Are the things that were said false, then? “No,” he says. “He did come into Palestine, but he did not see that as the promise. He longed for another, the one in heaven, and considered himself a stranger to all present things.” Paul bears witness to this when he adds: “And confessing that they were strangers and sojourners.” Tell me, is a man a stranger who received a homeland and so large a country? “Yes,” he says, “for he looked not to this but to heaven. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking another homeland, whose craftsman and builder is God”: that heavenly Jerusalem, the one above. Do you see how God promised him things perceived by the senses, and how he sought the Jerusalem above? “For those who say such things,” he says, “make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of the one they had left, they would have had the opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one.” So the promise was of things perceived by the senses, but the righteous man's desire was for things perceived by the mind. With us it is the opposite. To him God promised Palestine, and he gazed toward heaven; to us he promises heaven, and we gape at the earth. 5. This is what we have gained from Abraham's name. We have learned why he was called the man from beyond, and that he left his own land and moved to a foreign one. He passed by what was certain and looked to what was uncertain; he threw away what was in his hands and gaped after what lay in hope; he received things perceived by the senses and reached up toward things perceived by the mind. And he did all this before grace, before the law, before the teaching of the prophets. From this it is clear that he had no teacher. Nature was enough for him: it stirred up the reasonings of his conscience, and so he found God, the Creator of the universe. [?] he was called Abram, and that is why his parents gave him this name. But perhaps someone might say that this is false. Were Abraham's parents righteous? Were they pleasing to God? Did they know what was going to happen? Did they foresee the promise that the Master was going to speak? Were they not impious idolaters, the most barbarous of barbarians? I know that too, and that is exactly why I praise the righteous man: with such fathers he himself became such a man. This is the wonderful and astonishing thing, that a cultivated fruit was borne from a foreign and wild root. The wickedness of fathers is no charge against children who live in piety. Rather, if something wonderful must be said, it is even a cause for praise: they did not receive piety from their ancestors and had no one to guide them, yet, as if traveling through a trackless desert, they were able to find the road that leads to heaven. So having an impious father is no charge against anyone; imitating the father's impiety is. And the greatest reproach is not having bad parents, but failing to care for them and failing to do all we can to free them from their wickedness. When we have done everything we can for their souls and they still remain in their wickedness, we are free of all blame and accusation. I have said this, beloved, so that you will not be ashamed when you hear that Abraham had an impious father. For Timothy too had an impious father: he was the son of a Jewish woman [?]… flood, called him the one who gives rest.

6. To show that I am not forcing the interpretation, let us hear it from Scripture itself: “Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-eight years, and fathered a son, and called his name Noah, saying, ‘This one will give us rest from our labors, and our griefs, and the works of our hands, and from the ground which God has cursed.’” What are you saying, “He will give us rest”? And why did he not say, someone asks, “This one will kill us, this one will bring the flood about,” instead of saying, “He will give us rest”? The whole creation was dissolved into its elements. The deeps burst open below, the floodgates were opened above, and everything became one sea, strange, astonishing and terrifying. The bodies of men and the bodies of horses and wild beasts were hidden in a common tomb of mud. Tell me, do you call such great evils and such a disaster rest? “Yes,” he says. People were living in wickedness, and the flood cut their wickedness short, so those who were freed from wickedness found rest. A body gripped by many kinds of disease, for which no cure can be found, is given rest when death comes and takes it.
